reference.title: Crunch Floor (male)
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Waist, equipment Body weight, exercise type Strength

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl up, inhale as you lower. Do not hold the breath at the top.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s up, a short squeeze, about 1.5 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1 s up, brief pause, 1.5-2 s down
prescription.progression: Slower lowering and a 2 s hold, then arms overhead, then a light plate on the chest

cues.text: Lie on your back, knees bent about 90 degrees, feet flat and hip width. Fingertips lightly behind the head, elbows wide.
Breathe out and curl the head, shoulders and shoulder blades off the mat; ribs toward the hips.
Short squeeze at the top. Low back stays on the mat; the hands only support the head.
Breathe in and lower slowly, shoulder blades first, head last.
Head rests briefly; repeat without bouncing.

mistakes.mistake: Pulling on the neck with the hands
mistakes.fix: Fingertips only and elbows wide; or cross the arms on the chest.
Keep a fist-sized gap under the chin and look up toward the knees.

mistakes.mistake: Sitting all the way up (hip flexors take over)
mistakes.fix: Stop once the shoulder blades clear the mat; the low back stays down.
Control the lowering for about 1.5-2 s.

kinematics.measure: Upper trunk (T12 to C7) from the floor
kinematics.norm: Head, shoulders and shoulder blades clear the mat; no study fixes the angle (clinical opinion)
Small: about 3 degrees of lumbar flexion in a crunch, cited by Escamilla 2016 from earlier work
Most of the curl happens here (clinical opinion)
Knees about 90 degrees, feet flat; the pelvis and legs do not move (clinical opinion)
Neck flexes with the trunk; hands do not pull (clinical opinion)
Controlled, about 1 s up and 1.5-2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: Escamilla et al. 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379; PMC4922527)
Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
Sarti et al. 1996, muscle activity in upper and lower rectus abdominis during abdominal exercises (Arch Phys Med Rehabil 77(12):1293-1297; PMID 8976314)
Axler and McGill 1997, low-back loads over a variety of abdominal exercises: searching for the safest abdominal challenge (Med Sci Sports Exerc 29(6):804-811)
McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.

Low-back pain, disc problems or flexion intolerance: start with a McGill-style curl-up, dead bug or plank; partial curl-ups gave the best abdominal challenge for the least spine compression in one model study (Axler and McGill 1997).
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion or straight-leg work.
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture: avoid repeated loaded spinal flexion.
modify: Neck pain: cross the arms on the chest or rest the head on a folded towel; reduce the range.
Keep total flexion reps moderate across a session.
regressions: McGill curl-up (one knee bent, hands under the low back, head and shoulders lift only a little).
Smaller range: head and shoulders only.
progressions: Slow 3 s lowering with a 2 s hold.
Light plate held on the chest.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the ribs toward the pelvis: about 53% MVIC upper and 39% lower rectus in a crunch (Escamilla 2016); about 52% MVC in a straight curl-up (Konrad 2001). The curl-up favoured the upper portion in people who performed it correctly (Sarti 1996).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: External and internal obliques assist trunk flexion (about 28% and 33% MVIC in a crunch, Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: External and internal obliques assist trunk flexion (about 28% and 33% MVIC in a crunch, Escamilla 2016).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Stay quiet: rectus femoris was only about 6% MVIC in a crunch (Escamilla 2016), and curl-ups gave the lowest psoas challenge of the tasks McGill compared (McGill 1998). They only steady the bent legs.
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Stay quiet: rectus femoris was only about 6% MVIC in a crunch (Escamilla 2016), and curl-ups gave the lowest psoas challenge of the tasks McGill compared (McGill 1998). They only steady the bent legs.
